gloss: To come to believe that something is true, or to agree to take what is offered.
examples: I *accept* that we may never know the whole story.
She *accepted* the job offer on Friday.
They have *accepted* our explanation without argument.

gloss: To admit that something is true or that someone deserves attention.
examples: Both sides *acknowledge* that the talks have stalled.
He *acknowledged* his mistake in front of the whole team.
The company has never *acknowledged* the problem.

gloss: To examine something in detail in order to understand how it works.
examples: Let us *analyze* the numbers before we decide.
The lab *analyzed* the water samples overnight.
She is *analyzing* the survey results right now.
contrast: American *analyze*; British *analyse*.

gloss: To expect something and get ready for it.
examples: Good drivers *anticipate* what other cars will do.
Nobody *anticipated* such a long delay.
We are *anticipating* a busy weekend.

gloss: To judge the quality, size, or value of something.
examples: Teachers *assess* each student twice a year.
The inspector *assessed* the damage in an hour.
The risk has not been properly *assessed*.

gloss: To accept that something is true without proof.
examples: Do not *assume* that everyone has read the email.
I *assumed* you were coming with us.
We had *assumed* the store was open on Sundays.

transitivity: both — transitive (I believe you), intransitive (seeing is believing)
gloss: To think that something is true or that someone is telling the truth.
examples: I *believe* she is telling the truth.
Nobody *believed* his story at first.
He has always *believed* in working hard.
contrast: *believe someone* = верить кому-то; *believe in someone* = верить в кого-то.

transitivity: both — transitive (brainstorm ideas), intransitive (let us brainstorm)
gloss: To think up as many ideas as possible, usually with other people.
examples: Let us *brainstorm* a few titles for the article.
We *brainstormed* for an hour and filled two whiteboards.
They are *brainstorming* names for the new product.

gloss: To work something out using numbers.
examples: The app *calculates* the tip for you.
I *calculated* the cost per person.
Shipping has already been *calculated*.

gloss: To say that something is true without proving it.
examples: They *claim* the recipe is two hundred years old.
He *claimed* he had never seen the document.
The seller is *claiming* that the damage happened in transit.

gloss: To make something easier to understand.
examples: Could you *clarify* the second rule?
Her email *clarified* the deadline.
The point has been *clarified* twice already.
contrast: The -y turns into -ies and -ied: *clarifies*, *clarified*.

gloss: To put people or things into groups by type.
examples: Libraries *classify* books by subject.
The doctor *classified* the case as mild.
These documents are *classified* as secret.
contrast: The -y turns into -ies and -ied: *classifies*, *classified*.

transitivity: both — transitive (compare prices), intransitive (how do the two compare?)
gloss: To look at two or more things in order to see how they are alike or different.
examples: *Compare* the two offers before you sign anything.
We *compared* prices at three stores.
This car is often *compared* to a small SUV.
contrast: *compare to* points out a likeness; *compare with* weighs two things side by side.

gloss: To understand something fully, especially something difficult; a formal word where speech would use understand.
examples: Few people *comprehend* how large that number really is.
She *comprehended* the danger at once.
He sat there, not *comprehending* a word.

transitivity: both — transitive (conceive a plan), intransitive (conceive of a world without money)
gloss: To form an idea or a plan in your mind.
examples: I cannot *conceive* of a simpler solution.
She *conceived* the whole project on a train ride.
The bridge was *conceived* in the 1930s.
contrast: After c the spelling is -ei-: *conceive*, *receive*, *perceive*.

transitivity: both — transitive (concede a point), intransitive (he conceded at last)
gloss: To admit that something is true, often unwillingly.
examples: I *concede* that the price is fair.
The candidate *conceded* on election night.
Having *conceded* the point, he changed the subject.

transitivity: both — transitive (concentrate your efforts), intransitive (I cannot concentrate)
gloss: To give all your attention to one thing.
examples: I cannot *concentrate* with the TV on.
She *concentrated* on the hardest questions first.
He was *concentrating* so hard that he did not hear me.
contrast: You *concentrate on* something, never concentrate at something.

transitivity: both — transitive (conclude the meeting), intransitive (the study concluded)
gloss: To decide that something is true after thinking about the facts.
examples: What do you *conclude* from these numbers?
The jury *concluded* that he was innocent.
Researchers have *concluded* that the drug is safe.

gloss: To show or state that something is definitely true.
examples: Please *confirm* your address.
The lab *confirmed* the results yesterday.
Your reservation has been *confirmed*.

gloss: To mix one thing up with another, or to make someone unable to think clearly.
examples: People often *confuse* the two brothers.
The map only *confused* us more.
I am always *confusing* their names.
contrast: You *confuse* one thing *with* another.

gloss: To think carefully about something before deciding, or to hold an opinion about it.
examples: We *consider* him the best teacher in the school.
They *considered* three cities before choosing Denver.
She is *considering* moving back home.
contrast: *consider doing* something, never consider to do something.

transitivity: both — transitive (consult a doctor), intransitive (consult with a lawyer)
gloss: To go to someone or something for advice or information.
examples: Always *consult* a doctor before starting a diet.
We *consulted* the map twice and still got lost.
He is *consulting* with his lawyer this week.
contrast: *consult someone* directly, or *consult with* someone to talk it over.

gloss: To think about something long and seriously.
examples: He likes to *contemplate* such questions on long walks.
She *contemplated* quitting, then stayed another year.
They are *contemplating* a move to Texas.
contrast: *contemplate doing* something, not contemplate to do something.

gloss: To say the opposite of what someone else has said, or to go against a fact.
examples: The two reports *contradict* each other.
He *contradicted* his own story twice.
She has never *contradicted* her boss in public.

gloss: To make someone believe that something is true.
examples: You will never *convince* him to fly.
Her argument *convinced* the whole committee.
I am not *convinced* that the price is fair.
contrast: *convince someone of* something, or *convince someone that* something is so.

transitivity: both — transitive (debate the issue), intransitive (they debated for hours)
gloss: To discuss opposing ideas, or to turn a decision over in your mind.
examples: The senators will *debate* the bill on Tuesday.
I *debated* whether to call her back.
They are still *debating* the wording.

transitivity: both — transitive (decide the winner), intransitive (you decide)
gloss: To make a choice after thinking about it.
examples: You *decide* where we eat tonight.
We *decided* to take the early flight.
Nothing has been *decided* yet.
contrast: *decide to do* something; *decide on* a thing.

gloss: To work something out from the facts you already have.
examples: From the ashes you can *deduce* what burned.
She *deduced* his age from his school photos.
Little can be *deduced* from a single bad test.

gloss: To consider something to be a certain way, in formal or official language.
examples: The court may *deem* the contract invalid.
Officials *deemed* the building unsafe.
The proposal was *deemed* too expensive.

gloss: To say exactly what a word means or what something is.
examples: How would you *define* success?
The law *defined* the term very narrowly.
Her role has never been clearly *defined*.

gloss: To show clearly that something is true, or to show how something works.
examples: These numbers *demonstrate* the problem better than words do.
He *demonstrated* the machine for us.
The study has *demonstrated* a clear link.

gloss: To say that something is not true.
examples: They *deny* any connection to the company.
He *denied* everything at the hearing.
She is *denying* that she ever saw the email.
contrast: The -y turns into -ies and -ied: *denies*, *denied*.

gloss: To say what someone or something is like.
examples: Can you *describe* the man you saw?
She *described* the house in detail.
The town has been *described* as sleepy.
contrast: *describe something to someone*: describe the room to me, not describe me the room.

gloss: To notice something that is hard to see, hear, or measure.
examples: Dogs can *detect* smells we cannot.
I *detected* a note of doubt in her voice.
No errors were *detected* in the code.

gloss: To find out something for certain, or to settle it.
examples: Tests will *determine* the cause.
The judge *determined* that the search was legal.
The route has not been *determined* yet.

gloss: To invent a plan, a system, or a method.
examples: We need to *devise* a fairer schedule.
He *devised* a way to cut the wait in half.
They are *devising* a new grading system.
contrast: The verb *devise* ends in a /z/ sound; the noun *device* ends in /s/.

gloss: To have a different opinion from someone else.
examples: I *disagree* with almost everything in that article.
The two doctors *disagreed* about the diagnosis.
They have been *disagreeing* about this for years.
contrast: The -ee stays and you just add -d: *disagreed*. You *disagree with* a person, *about* a thing.

gloss: To find out about something for the first time.
examples: Kids *discover* something new every day.
We *discovered* the leak too late.
A second entrance has been *discovered*.

gloss: To decide that an idea or a person is not worth taking seriously.
examples: Do not *dismiss* the idea so quickly.
He *dismissed* my worries with a laugh.
The complaint was *dismissed* by the court.

transitivity: both — transitive (distinguish the twins), intransitive (distinguish between them)
gloss: To see or explain the difference between things.
examples: Can you *distinguish* the twins?
She *distinguished* the real bills from the fakes.
Young children have trouble *distinguishing* between fact and fantasy.
contrast: *distinguish between* two things, or *distinguish* one *from* another.

gloss: To think that something is probably not true or will probably not happen.
examples: I *doubt* he will call back.
Nobody *doubted* her honesty.
He has never *doubted* his own judgment.
contrast: The b is silent: DOWT. The same silent b appears in *debt* and *subtle*.

gloss: To picture in your mind how something could be in the future.
examples: I *envision* a small shop with two or three tables.
The founders *envisioned* a free library in every town.
The park is *envisioned* as a green corridor.

gloss: To make a rough judgment about an amount, a size, or a cost.
examples: Can you *estimate* how long the drive takes?
The contractor *estimated* six weeks of work.
Damage is *estimated* at two million dollars.
contrast: The verb is ES-tuh-mayt; the noun *estimate* ends in a schwa: ES-tuh-muht.

gloss: To judge carefully how good or how useful something is.
examples: We *evaluate* every applicant the same way.
The team *evaluated* four suppliers.
The program is being *evaluated* this fall.

gloss: To look at something closely in order to learn about it.
examples: Let us *examine* the contract line by line.
The doctor *examined* her knee.
The evidence has been *examined* by two experts.

gloss: To believe that something will happen or that someone will do something.
examples: We *expect* about thirty guests.
I *expected* the test to be harder.
Rain is *expected* by evening.
contrast: *expect someone to do* something: I expect you to be on time.

gloss: To make something clear by describing it in detail.
examples: Could you *explain* the rules again?
She *explained* why the flight was canceled.
He has *explained* it three times already.
contrast: *explain something to someone*, never explain me something.

transitivity: both — transitive (explore the city), intransitive (we went exploring)
gloss: To look into a place or an idea to find out what is there.
examples: The book *explores* what memory really is.
We *explored* the old town on foot.
They are *exploring* several options.

transitivity: both — transitive (fear the worst), intransitive (never fear)
gloss: To be afraid of something, or to believe with worry that it is true.
examples: Many parents *fear* that the school will close.
We *feared* the worst when the phone rang at three in the morning.
Twelve people are *feared* missing.

transitivity: both — transitive (focus the camera), intransitive (focus on the task)
gloss: To give your attention to one thing rather than to many.
examples: Let us *focus* on the first chapter.
He *focused* on his breathing and calmed down.
She is *focusing* on her health this year.
contrast: American English keeps one s: *focused*, *focusing*. You *focus on* something.

gloss: To understand an idea, especially a difficult one.
examples: It took me a while to *grasp* what she meant.
He never really *grasped* the math behind it.
The rule is easily *grasped* once you see an example.

transitivity: both — transitive (guess the answer), intransitive (go ahead and guess)
gloss: To give an answer you are not sure of, or to suppose something.
examples: I *guess* we should leave now.
You *guessed* the number on the first try.
I was only *guessing*, and I got lucky.
contrast: The third person adds -es: *guesses*.

gloss: To pause before doing something because you are unsure.
examples: Do not *hesitate* to call if you need help.
She *hesitated* for a second, then signed.
He is still *hesitating* over the price.
contrast: *hesitate to do* something.

transitivity: both — transitive (I hope so), intransitive (we can only hope)
gloss: To want something to happen and believe that it might.
examples: We *hope* to see you in June.
I *hoped* the rain would stop.
She is *hoping* for a scholarship.
contrast: Drop the e: *hoping*, not hopeing. You *hope for* a thing and *hope to do* something.

gloss: To recognize who or what someone or something is.
examples: Can you *identify* the plant from this photo?
Witnesses *identified* the car right away.
The victims have not been *identified*.
contrast: The -y turns into -ies and -ied: *identifies*, *identified*.

gloss: To pay no attention to someone or something on purpose.
examples: Just *ignore* the noise from upstairs.
He *ignored* three warning emails.
The advice was *ignored* completely.

gloss: To form a picture of something in your mind.
examples: *Imagine* a city with no cars.
I *imagined* the room much bigger.
She is *imagining* problems that do not exist.
contrast: *imagine doing* something, not imagine to do something.

gloss: To suggest something without saying it directly.
examples: Silence does not always *imply* agreement.
His tone *implied* that he did not believe me.
Are you *implying* that I lied?
contrast: The speaker *implies*; the listener *infers*. The -y turns into -ies and -ied.

gloss: To show that something is true or likely.
examples: These symptoms *indicate* a mild infection.
The survey *indicated* strong support.
Nothing has *indicated* a problem so far.

gloss: To reach a conclusion from evidence rather than from a direct statement.
examples: What do you *infer* from her silence?
The reader *inferred* that the narrator had died.
We are *inferring* a lot from very little data.
contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the r doubles: *inferred*, *inferring*.

gloss: To say firmly that something is true or that it must happen.
examples: They *insist* on paying for dinner.
She *insisted* that we take the car.
He is *insisting* on an apology.
contrast: *insist on* something, or *insist that* something happen.

gloss: To plan to do something.
examples: We *intend* to stay two nights.
I never *intended* to hurt anyone.
The room was *intended* as a nursery.
contrast: *intend to do* something.

gloss: To decide what something means, or to put speech into another language.
examples: Courts *interpret* the law, they do not write it.
She *interpreted* his silence as anger.
He is *interpreting* for the visiting team.
contrast: The t does not double, because the stress is not on the last syllable: *interpreted*.

gloss: To think up something that did not exist before, including a false story.
examples: Kids *invent* games out of nothing.
He *invented* an excuse on the spot.
The zipper was *invented* over a century ago.

transitivity: both — transitive (investigate a crime), intransitive (police are investigating)
gloss: To try to find out the truth about something by examining it.
examples: Reporters *investigate* stories like this for months.
The city *investigated* the complaint and found nothing.
Two agencies are *investigating* the crash.

transitivity: both — transitive (judge a contest), intransitive (judging by his face)
gloss: To form an opinion about someone or something after thinking about it.
examples: Do not *judge* a book by its cover.
She *judged* the distance perfectly.
*Judging* by the sky, it will rain before noon.
contrast: Drop the e: *judging*, not judgeing.

gloss: To show that something is right or reasonable.
examples: Nothing can *justify* lying to them.
He *justified* the cost by pointing to the savings.
Her anger was completely *justified*.
contrast: The -y turns into -ies and -ied: *justifies*, *justified*.

gloss: To learn something so well that you can repeat it from memory.
examples: You do not need to *memorize* the formula.
He *memorized* the whole speech in two days.
She is *memorizing* her lines for the play.
contrast: American *memorize*; British *memorise*.

gloss: To notice something and mention or record it.
examples: Please *note* the change of address.
The report *noted* several small errors.
As *noted* above, the rules changed in May.

gloss: To see, hear, or become aware of something.
examples: Did you *notice* anything strange?
I *noticed* that the light was still on.
Nobody had *noticed* the mistake until then.
contrast: Drop the e: *noticing*, not noticeing.

gloss: To watch something carefully, or to remark on what you see.
examples: Student teachers *observe* a classroom before they teach in one.
He *observed* that nobody had touched the food.
The birds are being *observed* from a hide.

gloss: To fail to notice something, or to decide to let a fault pass.
examples: It is easy to *overlook* a typo in your own writing.
The auditors *overlooked* two payments.
Her best work has been *overlooked* for years.
contrast: One word, not a phrasal verb: you *overlook* a detail, but you *look over* a document to check it.

gloss: To notice something with the senses, or to understand it in a certain way.
examples: Dogs *perceive* sounds we cannot hear.
She *perceived* at once that something was wrong.
The delay was *perceived* as an insult.
contrast: After c the spelling is -ei-: *perceive*, *receive*, *deceive*.

gloss: To make someone agree to do something by giving reasons.
examples: See if you can *persuade* her to stay.
He *persuaded* the bank to lower the rate.
I am not *persuaded* by that argument.
contrast: *persuade someone to do* something.

gloss: To form an image of something in your mind.
examples: *Picture* a beach with nobody on it.
I *pictured* the house as much older.
She is *picturing* herself on stage.
contrast: *picture someone doing* something: I can picture him teaching.

transitivity: both — transitive (plan a trip), intransitive (plan ahead)
gloss: To decide in advance how something will be done.
examples: We *plan* to leave at six.
They *planned* the wedding in three months.
She is *planning* a trip to Alaska.
contrast: One vowel plus one consonant, so the n doubles: *planned*, *planning*.

transitivity: both — transitive (ponder the question), intransitive (ponder over a problem)
gloss: To think about something slowly and seriously.
examples: He likes to *ponder* such questions on long walks.
She *pondered* the offer for a week.
They sat *pondering* what to do next.

gloss: To say what you think will happen in the future.
examples: Nobody can *predict* the weather a month out.
He *predicted* the score almost exactly.
A mild winter has been *predicted*.

gloss: To like one thing more than another.
examples: I *prefer* tea to coffee.
She *preferred* the second draft.
He has always *preferred* working at night.
contrast: The r doubles in *preferred* and *preferring*, but not in the noun *preference*.

gloss: To suppose that something is true because it is likely.
examples: I *presume* you have already eaten.
The police *presumed* the car was stolen.
He is *presumed* innocent until proven guilty.

transitivity: both — transitive (pretend to be asleep), intransitive (children love to pretend)
gloss: To act as if something is true when it is not.
examples: Do not *pretend* you did not hear me.
He *pretended* to be asleep.
She is only *pretending* to be angry.
contrast: *pretend to be* something, or *pretend that* something is so.

ru: расставлять приоритеты, ставить на первое место
transitivity: both — transitive (prioritize safety), intransitive (learn to prioritize)
gloss: To decide which things matter most and deal with them first.
examples: You have to *prioritize* when the list gets long.
We *prioritized* the bugs that block users.
Safety is being *prioritized* over speed.
contrast: American *prioritize*; British *prioritise*.

gloss: To put forward an idea or a plan for others to consider.
examples: I *propose* that we vote on it now.
The mayor *proposed* a new bus line.
Two changes have been *proposed*.

gloss: To express doubt about something, or to ask someone about it.
examples: Nobody dares to *question* his decisions.
Police *questioned* three witnesses.
She is *questioning* whether the job is worth it.

gloss: To become aware of something you had not understood before.
examples: I *realize* this is hard to hear.
She *realized* that her keys were still inside.
He had not *realized* how late it was.
contrast: American *realize*; British *realise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (he reasoned that it was safe), intransitive (reason with him)
gloss: To think logically about something in order to reach a conclusion.
examples: Try to *reason* with her before you give up.
He *reasoned* that the store would still be open.
She is *reasoning* from a single example.
contrast: You *reason with* a person you hope to convince.

gloss: To bring something back into your mind, a little more formally than remember.
examples: I cannot *recall* his last name.
She *recalled* the address perfectly.
He has *recalled* very little about that night.

gloss: To think or suppose something, especially in informal speech.
examples: I *reckon* we can be there by noon.
He *reckoned* the trip would take six hours.
They are *reckoning* on a hundred guests.

gloss: To know someone or something because you have met it before, or to admit that it is real.
examples: I did not *recognize* you with the beard.
She *recognized* his voice at once.
The state has *recognized* the marriage.
contrast: American *recognize*; British *recognise*. The g is pronounced: REK-uhg-nyz.

transitivity: both — transitive (reconsider the offer), intransitive (please reconsider)
gloss: To think about a decision again and possibly change it.
examples: I hope you will *reconsider*.
The board *reconsidered* and voted again.
They are *reconsidering* the whole plan.

transitivity: both — transitive (the price reflects demand), intransitive (reflect on the year)
gloss: To think quietly and seriously about something.
examples: Take a week to *reflect* on the offer.
He *reflected* on how much had changed.
She is *reflecting* on twenty years of teaching.
contrast: You *reflect on* a subject.

transitivity: both — transitive (refuse an offer), intransitive (he simply refused)
gloss: To say firmly that you will not do or accept something.
examples: They *refuse* to discuss the price.
She *refused* the invitation politely.
He is *refusing* to sign anything.
contrast: The verb is rih-FYOOZ; the noun *refuse* (мусор) is REF-yoos.

gloss: To consider someone or something in a particular way.
examples: Many *regard* her as the best coach in the league.
He *regarded* the whole thing as a joke.
The book is widely *regarded* as a classic.
contrast: *regard someone as* something, not regard someone like something.

gloss: To feel sorry about something you did or failed to do.
examples: You will *regret* it if you skip the trip.
She *regretted* the email the moment she sent it.
He has always *regretted* leaving school early.
contrast: The stress falls on the last syllable, so the t doubles: *regretted*, *regretting*.

gloss: To refuse to accept an idea, an offer, or a person.
examples: Editors *reject* most of what they receive.
The bank *rejected* our application.
His appeal has been *rejected* twice.
contrast: The verb is rih-JEKT; the noun *reject* is REE-jekt.

gloss: To depend on someone or something to work or to help.
examples: Small towns *rely* on volunteers.
We *relied* on his map and got lost.
She is *relying* on you to be there.
contrast: Always *rely on*. The -y turns into -ies and -ied: *relies*, *relied*.

transitivity: both — transitive (remember his name), intransitive (if I remember right)
gloss: To keep something in your mind or bring it back to mind.
examples: I *remember* the summer we spent there.
He *remembered* the password on the third try.
She is *remembering* it wrong.
contrast: *remember to do* = не забыть сделать; *remember doing* = помнить, как делал.

gloss: To make someone think of something they might forget, or of someone else.
examples: *Remind* me to buy milk.
She *reminded* him about the meeting.
You have *reminded* me of my grandfather.
contrast: You *remember* something yourself; you *remind* another person of it.

transitivity: both — transitive (research a topic), intransitive (research into the causes)
gloss: To study a subject carefully in order to find out new facts.
examples: Always *research* a company before the interview.
She *researched* the family tree for years.
He is *researching* rural schools in Ohio.
contrast: The third person adds -es: *researches*.

gloss: To settle a problem or an argument, or to decide firmly to do something.
examples: We need to *resolve* this before Friday.
They *resolved* the dispute out of court.
The issue has been *resolved*.

gloss: To look at something again in order to check or judge it.
examples: Let us *review* the numbers one more time.
The committee *reviewed* all forty applications.
Your case is being *reviewed*.

gloss: To change a text, a plan, or an opinion after thinking again.
examples: I need to *revise* the second paragraph.
They *revised* the budget twice.
The forecast has been *revised* downward.
contrast: In American English *revise* means to change something; British students also use it for studying before an exam.

gloss: To plan that something will happen at a particular time.
examples: Can we *schedule* the call for Tuesday?
They *scheduled* the surgery for April.
The flight is *scheduled* to land at noon.
contrast: Americans say SKEJ-ool; the British say SHED-yool.

gloss: To choose someone or something carefully from a group, a little more formally than choose.
examples: *Select* three photos for the front page.
The coach *selected* two new players.
She has been *selected* for the program.

gloss: To feel or notice something without being told.
examples: Dogs *sense* fear.
I *sensed* that he wanted to leave.
She is *sensing* trouble ahead.

gloss: To find the answer to a problem or a puzzle.
examples: Money alone will not *solve* this.
He *solved* the puzzle in four minutes.
The case was never *solved*.
contrast: You *solve* a puzzle or an equation; you *resolve* an argument.

gloss: To guess about something without having enough facts.
examples: I will not *speculate* about the cause.
Reporters *speculated* for days about her plans.
Everyone is *speculating* about who will get the job.
contrast: You *speculate about* or *on* something.

gloss: To notice someone or something, often suddenly.
examples: See if you can *spot* the difference.
He *spotted* the error on page two.
She was *spotted* leaving the building.
contrast: One vowel plus one consonant, so the t doubles: *spotted*, *spotting*.

gloss: To say or write something clearly and formally.
examples: Please *state* your name for the record.
The letter *stated* that the account was closed.
As *stated* earlier, the deadline has not changed.

transitivity: both — transitive (study medicine), intransitive (study for a test)
gloss: To spend time learning about a subject, or to look at something closely.
examples: He wants to *study* engineering.
She *studied* the menu for five minutes.
They are *studying* for finals.
contrast: The -y turns into -ies and -ied: *studies*, *studied*, but *studying* keeps the y.

gloss: To put forward an idea, or to show that something is probably true.
examples: Can you *suggest* a good dentist?
The data *suggested* a slow recovery.
It has been *suggested* that we meet monthly.
contrast: *suggest something to someone*, never suggest me a restaurant.

gloss: To give the main points of something in a short form.
examples: Can you *summarize* the article in two sentences?
She *summarized* the meeting in one paragraph.
The findings are *summarized* on page one.
contrast: American *summarize*; British *summarise*.

gloss: To think that something is probably true.
examples: I *suppose* you are right.
Everyone *supposed* the meeting was canceled.
You are *supposed* to check in an hour early.
contrast: *be supposed to* = должен, полагается: he is supposed to call.

gloss: To think that something is probably true or that someone is probably guilty.
examples: I *suspect* she already knows.
Doctors *suspected* the flu at first.
He is *suspected* of taking the money.
contrast: The verb is suh-SPEKT; the noun *suspect* is SUS-pekt.

transitivity: both — transitive (trust your doctor), intransitive (trust in the process)
gloss: To believe that someone is honest or that something is safe.
examples: I *trust* him with the keys.
She *trusted* the directions and ended up lost.
He is *trusted* by everyone on the team.

gloss: To check that something is true or accurate.
examples: Please *verify* the spelling of the name.
The bank *verified* my identity by phone.
The story has not been *verified*.
contrast: The -y turns into -ies and -ied: *verifies*, *verified*.

gloss: To form a clear picture of something in your mind.
examples: Try to *visualize* the finished room.
He *visualized* the jump before every attempt.
She is *visualizing* the route step by step.
contrast: American *visualize*; British *visualise*.

gloss: To think carefully about the good and bad sides of something.
examples: *Weigh* the costs against the benefits.
They *weighed* two offers before choosing.
Every option has been carefully *weighed*.
contrast: The gh is silent: WAY. The past is *weighed*, not weighted.

transitivity: both — transitive (wish you luck), intransitive (wish for nothing)
gloss: To want something that is unlikely or impossible.
examples: I *wish* I had more time.
She *wished* him luck and left.
He is *wishing* for snow on his birthday.
contrast: The third person adds -es: *wishes*. After *wish* use a past form: I wish I knew.

transitivity: both — transitive (I wonder what happened), intransitive (it makes you wonder)
gloss: To want to know something, or to ask yourself about it.
examples: I *wonder* what happened to them.
She *wondered* whether to say anything.
We were *wondering* if you could help.
contrast: *wonder* WUN-dur = задаваться вопросом; *wander* WAHN-dur = бродить.

transitivity: both — transitive (it worries me), intransitive (do not worry)
gloss: To think about a problem in a way that makes you anxious.
examples: Do not *worry* about the test.
He *worried* all night about the results.
She has been *worrying* about money.
contrast: The -y turns into -ies and -ied: *worries*, *worried*. You *worry about* something.
